Case Vignette: Mr. L.

Mr. L. is a 67-year-old widowed man, a retired military medic, who presents for his third session. He sits upright in the chair, hands resting on his knees, as if waiting for an order. He speaks in a low, measured voice, often pausing to rub his left shoulder, a gesture that has become more frequent as our sessions progress.

The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, on a rainy Tuesday afternoon. Mr. L. was driving home from the VA clinic, a routine trip he had made hundreds of times. He was stopped at a red light when a pickup truck, later determined to have blown a tire, crossed the median and struck his sedan head-on at approximately forty-five miles per hour. He remembers the sound-a deep, wet crunch-and the sensation of the steering column pressing into his chest. His seatbelt locked, but his head struck the side window, fracturing his orbital bone. He was conscious throughout.

His training as a medic took over. He remembers checking his own pulse, feeling for blood, assessing his own airway. He remembers the smell of gasoline and the hiss of steam from the ruptured radiator. He remembers the driver of the other truck, a young man, staggering toward his window, screaming for help. Mr. L. could not move. He could not get out of the car. He could only lie there, watching the young man's face contort, and think, I am supposed to save him. This is what I do. And I cannot move.

He was extricated by the fire department and hospitalized for three days with a concussion, three broken ribs, and a fractured clavicle. The physical wounds healed. But something else did not.

In the months that followed, Mr. L. began to avoid driving. At first, it was just the intersection where the accident occurred. Then it was any intersection with a traffic light. Then it was highways. Now, he will only drive on residential streets, and only during daylight hours. He takes back roads that double his commute to the grocery store. He has not visited his daughter, who lives forty minutes away, in over a year. He tells me, "I know it's irrational. I was a medic. I saw worse. But my body doesn't care what my head knows."

He experiences intrusive memories several times a day. They are not flashbacks in the cinematic sense-he does not feel he is back in the car. Instead, they are sudden, vivid replays: the sound of the impact, the smell of gasoline, the young man's face. These intrusions are often triggered by the sound of a car horn, a sudden braking noise, or the sight of a pickup truck in his peripheral vision. When this happens, his heart races, his palms sweat, and he feels a tightness in his chest that he recognizes from his training as the beginning of a panic response. He has learned to pull over, to breathe, to wait it out. But he cannot stop the vigilance.

He sleeps poorly. He wakes multiple times a night from dreams of being trapped, of failing to help, of the young man's face turning into the faces of soldiers he could not save decades ago in Vietnam. He has not slept through the night since the accident. He avoids the news, especially stories about car accidents. He has stopped watching action movies, which he once enjoyed. He finds himself scanning every parking lot for erratic drivers, every intersection for potential hazards.

He describes himself as "on a short fuse." He snapped at a cashier last week for a minor delay. He feels guilty about it, but he cannot seem to control his startle response. He feels disconnected from his daughter and his grandchildren, as if a pane of glass has been placed between him and the rest of the world. He says, "I used to be the one who helped. Now I'm the one who needs help. And I don't know how to do that."

His PCL-5 score is 64, indicating a high level of PTSD symptom severity. He has stopped attending his weekly coffee group with other veterans. He spends most of his time at home, in his recliner, with the television on low, waiting for the day to pass.
